rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: Fed Dec hike ~68% (from ~80%); ECB Dec ~89%; BoJ Dec ~80%; BoC Dec ~56%; BoE 4.00% after Nov 5 hike; RBNZ Dec <50%
rows.read: Most big central banks still lean toward raising rates, led by the Bank of England's hike on Thursday. The stock slump has trimmed bets that the Federal Reserve hikes in December, which narrows one of the dollar's supports. Today's US jobs report will show whether that holds.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: US payrolls Oct fcst 65K (Sep 29K), unemployment fcst 4.2%; Canada jobs fcst +14.6K (Sep −68.3K); US jobless claims 189K (Nov 5)
rows.read: Layoffs in the US remain rare, but hiring has been slow, so today's jobs report is the key check on the economy. Canada needs a rebound after losing jobs in September. A falling stock market could also start to weigh on spending if it lasts.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: Brent ~$99.7 (+1.8%); euro-area CPI 4.0% Oct; BoE sees UK CPI near 5% by mid-2027; UMich 1-yr expectations prior 4.7%
rows.read: Oil climbed back toward $100, so the energy push on prices has not gone away. That keeps central banks in Europe, the UK and Canada worried about inflation. US households' own inflation expectations, out this morning, are the next read.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.figure: Nikkei −6.1%, Kospi ~−6%, ASX −0.5% (Nov 6); Nasdaq −5.5%, S&P 500 −4.4%, VIX ~28 (Nov 5); AUD/USD ~0.6916; NZD/USD ~0.5565
rows.read: The selloff in AI and chip stocks spread from Wall Street to Asia, where Japan's and South Korea's markets fell hardest. The Australian and New Zealand dollars took the hit, while the yen and the US dollar held up. If European and US stocks keep falling today, fear becomes the main driver for currencies again.

rows.title: Terms of Trade
rows.figure: Brent ~$99.7 (+1.8%), WTI ~$91.4 (+0.8%); Brent heading for ~12% weekly fall; Iran nuclear proposal sent via Qatar
rows.read: Oil rose a second day as tanker attacks near the Strait of Hormuz continued, even after Iran sent the US a proposal for talks. That raises the energy bill for importers like Japan and the euro area. Exporters like Canada would normally gain, but the global stock slump mattered more overnight.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: CFTC Oct 27: funds strongly against CAD, against EUR (real money for), against NZD and CHF, for AUD (real money strongly against), strongly for gold; new report Fri Nov 6, 2:30 PM CT
rows.read: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar and also bet against the euro and the kiwi. They still lean toward the Aussie while real money investors bet heavily against it, so this week's Aussie slide hurts the funds' side. Fresh figures arrive this afternoon.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: Canada 2025–26 deficit C$39.3B (forecast C$66.9B); C$50–60B a year ahead; Democrats control House and Senate; France on negative outlook at Fitch and Moody's
rows.read: Canada's budget showed a smaller deficit than planned thanks to oil income, and markets barely reacted. A Democratic Congress makes President Trump's spending plans harder to pass, which trims support for the dollar. France's debt worries still weigh on the euro.
